section.title: Malta and the Arrival in Rome
section.sectionRationale: The book reaches its goal. After Malta, where a viper cannot harm Paul and God heals through him, the company finally comes to Rome. There Paul reasons with the Jewish leaders, some believe and some do not, and Luke lets the ancient warning of Isaiah frame the turn to the Gentiles. Acts closes not with Paul's death but with the gospel preached boldly and unhindered in the capital of the world, its story deliberately left open.
section.thesis: Preserved through snakebite and sea, Paul comes at last to Rome, where he lays the risen Christ before Israel from Moses and the Prophets; and though some will not believe, God's salvation goes to the Gentiles, and the word is proclaimed in the heart of the empire boldly and without hindrance.
section.frameNote: Five movements: Paul unharmed by the viper on Malta; the healings that follow; the journey on to Rome and the welcome of the brothers; Paul's reasoning with the Roman Jews; and Isaiah's warning, the turn to the Gentiles, and the open ending of the gospel preached unhindered.

units.label: Ashore on Malta
units.note: the viper that could not harm him

verses.text: Once we were safely ashore, we learned that the island was called Malta.
The islanders showed us extraordinary kindness. They kindled a fire and welcomed all of us because it was raining and cold.
Paul gathered a bundle of sticks, and as he laid them on the fire, a viper, driven out by the heat, fastened itself to his hand.
When the islanders saw the creature hanging from his hand, they said to one another, “Surely this man is a murderer. Although he was saved from the sea, Justice has not allowed him to live.”
But Paul shook the creature off into the fire and suffered no ill effects.
The islanders were expecting him to swell up or suddenly drop dead. But after waiting a long time and seeing nothing unusual happen to him, they changed their minds and said he was a god.
Nearby stood an estate belonging to Publius, the chief official of the island. He welcomed us and entertained us hospitably for three days.
The father of Publius was sick in bed, suffering from fever and dysentery. Paul went in to see him, and after praying and placing his hands on him, he healed the man.
After this had happened, the rest of the sick on the island came and were cured as well.
The islanders honored us in many ways and supplied our needs when we were ready to sail.

units.label: The road to Rome
units.note: he was encouraged and gave thanks to God

verses.text: After three months we set sail in an Alexandrian ship that had wintered in the island. It had the Twin Brothers as a figurehead.
Putting in at Syracuse, we stayed there three days.
From there we weighed anchor and came to Rhegium. After one day, a south wind came up, and on the second day we arrived at Puteoli.
There we found some brothers who invited us to spend the week with them. And so we came to Rome.
The brothers there had heard about us and traveled as far as the Forum of Appius and the Three Taverns to meet us. When Paul saw them, he was encouraged and gave thanks to God.
When we arrived in Rome, Paul was permitted to stay by himself, with a soldier to guard him.

units.label: Paul reasons with the Jews of Rome
units.note: the kingdom of God, and Jesus from Moses and the Prophets

verses.text: After three days, he called together the leaders of the Jews. When they had gathered, he said to them, “Brothers, although I have done nothing against our people or the customs of our fathers, I was taken prisoner in Jerusalem and handed over to the Romans.
They examined me and wanted to release me, because there was no basis for a death sentence against me.
But when the Jews objected, I was compelled to appeal to Caesar, even though I have no charge to bring against my nation.
So for this reason I have called to see you and speak with you. It is because of the hope of Israel that I am bound with this chain.”
The leaders replied, “We have not received any letters about you from Judea, nor have any of the brothers from there reported or even mentioned anything bad about you.
But we consider your views worth hearing, because we know that people everywhere are speaking against this sect.”

So they set a day to meet with Paul, and many people came to the place he was staying. He expounded to them from morning to evening, testifying about the {{basileia|kingdom}} of God and persuading them about Jesus from the Law of Moses and the Prophets.
Some of them were convinced by what he said, but others refused to believe.

units.label: Isaiah's warning and the open ending
units.note: God's salvation sent to the Gentiles, proclaimed unhindered

verses.text: They disagreed among themselves and began to leave after Paul had made this final statement: “The Holy Spirit was right when He spoke to your fathers through Isaiah the prophet:
‘Go to this people and say, “You will be ever hearing but never understanding; you will be ever seeing but never perceiving.”

For this people’s heart has grown callous; they hardly hear with their ears, and they have closed their eyes. Otherwise they might see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their hearts, and turn, and I would heal them.’
Be advised, therefore, that God’s {{soterion|salvation}} has been sent to the Gentiles, and they will listen!”
Paul stayed there two full years in his own rented house, welcoming all who came to visit him.
{{parrhesia|Boldly}} and {{akolytos|freely}} he proclaimed the kingdom of God and taught about the Lord Jesus Christ.

basileia.gloss: Kingdom, kingly rule, reign. Acts opens and closes with the kingdom of God, Acts 1:3 and 28:31. Paul testifies to God's reign and persuades people about Jesus from the Scriptures, for the kingdom has come near in the crucified and risen King, and the gospel of the kingdom is now announced in Rome itself.

soterion.gloss: Salvation, God's saving deliverance. Paul declares that this salvation has been sent to the Gentiles, and they will listen. The word gathers up the whole aim of Acts, the good news of rescue in Christ, now going out beyond Israel to the nations, exactly as the prophets foretold.

parrhesia.gloss: Boldness, frank and open speech, freedom to say all. It is a keynote of Acts: the Spirit-filled church speaks the word with boldness. The book ends with Paul proclaiming Christ with this same parrhesia, undimmed by chains, a fitting close to the story of a gospel that will not be silenced.

akolytos.gloss: Without hindrance, unhindered. This is the very last word of Acts in the Greek. Though Paul is a prisoner awaiting Caesar, the word of God runs free. Luke ends not with a period on Paul's story but with the gospel advancing openly and unstoppably in the heart of the empire.

basic.context: The shipwrecked company lands on Malta, where a deadly viper fails to harm Paul and God heals many through him. After three months they sail on and finally reach Rome. There Paul, though a prisoner, gathers the Jewish leaders, explains his case, and spends a long day laying out the kingdom of God and Jesus from the Scriptures. Some believe, some do not, and Paul announces that salvation is going to the Gentiles. The book ends with him preaching freely for two years.
basic.hermeneutics: Read the ending as the deliberate climax of the whole book. Watch the Malta scene show God's protection and mercy, then the arrival fulfill the long promise of reaching Rome. The Isaiah quotation and the turn to the Gentiles gather up a theme that runs through all of Luke and Acts, and the final two verses, open and unfinished, are the point: the gospel goes on.
basic.originalLanguages: Paul testifies to the basileia, the kingdom, of God and persuades people about Jesus. He announces that God's soterion, salvation, has gone to the Gentiles. And the book ends with him preaching with parrhesia, boldness, and akolytos, without hindrance, the very last word of Acts.
basic.typology: The viper that cannot harm Paul recalls the promise that the seed of the woman would crush the serpent, and that God's servants would tread on serpents unharmed. Paul, bearing the gospel safely through venom and storm, pictures the church carrying Christ's victory over the ancient serpent to the nations.
basic.christ: Everything centers on Jesus. Paul preaches the kingdom of God and persuades people about Jesus from Moses and the Prophets, then teaches about the Lord Jesus Christ to all who come. The salvation sent to the Gentiles is salvation in Him. The risen and reigning Christ is the content of the message that fills the empire's capital.
basic.god: God keeps every promise. He preserved Paul through the sea, the snake, and the long road, and brought him to Rome to testify, just as He said. God's salvation, long promised to the nations, now goes out to the Gentiles, and His word cannot be bound even when His servant is. The whole story is the outworking of God's sovereign, saving purpose.
basic.crossReferences: Acts 1:8 set the program, witnesses to the ends of the earth. Isaiah 6:9 to 10 is the warning Paul quotes over unbelief. Luke 24:47 promised repentance preached to all nations. Romans, written earlier to this very city, unfolds the gospel Paul now preaches in Rome.
basic.oneStory: From Jerusalem to Rome, the risen Christ has poured out His Spirit and driven the gospel to the ends of the earth. The book ends with the word preached freely in the heart of the empire, its story left open because the mission is not finished; it continues through the church to this day.

context.literary:
The chapter is built in three panels, and each answers a different fear. On Malta, verses 1 to 10, the fear is that the sea has finished the mission; the panel shows God's care at work through Gentile kindness and through healing. On the road, verses 11 to 16, the fear is that the prisoner will arrive alone, and the panel is full of brothers who come out to meet him. In Rome, verses 17 to 31, the fear is that the Jewish people will close the door on the message, and the panel gives a mixed answer: some are convinced, some are not, and the word goes on.

The final scene is a well-marked pair of speeches. Paul's defence in verses 17 to 20 is a gentle one, calling the leaders 'brothers' and tying his chain to 'the hope of Israel.' Then, after a day of teaching, comes the Isaiah quotation of verses 25 to 28, which is the only truly solemn pronouncement in the chapter. Luke ends the book not on the speech but on the picture of verses 30 and 31, whose verbs describe continuing action: Paul 'welcomed' all who came, and 'proclaimed' and 'taught.'

The ending has an inclusio with the start of Acts. Acts 1:3 says Jesus spoke about 'the kingdom of God' to the apostles, and Acts 28:31 closes on Paul proclaiming 'the kingdom of God' and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ. The book that began with Jesus doing and teaching, Acts 1:1, ends with His servant doing and teaching in His name.

There is another echo in the three-fold pattern of Paul's turn to the Gentiles. At Pisidian Antioch he says 'we now turn to the Gentiles,' Acts 13:46, at Corinth 'from now on I will go to the Gentiles,' Acts 18:6, and here in Rome the same message is stated for the last time, verse 28. In each case the turn comes after a Jewish synagogue response that was divided, and in each case Jews continue to be reached after it. The pattern is a way of marking a direction, not a closing of a door.

Verse 29 is missing from the BSB because it appears in later manuscripts only, a note that the Jews left arguing among themselves.
context.historical:
The Mediterranean world Luke describes was a connected one. The ship that carries them from Malta is another Alexandrian vessel with the Twin Brothers, Castor and Pollux, as figurehead, verse 11. The BSB footnote names them as Greek gods, and sailors looked to them as protectors. Luke notes the detail without comment, as he does with the goddess Justice in verse 4, because the narrative is more interested in who actually protects Paul.

Malta was a Punic-speaking island under Roman rule. Luke calls its people by a Greek word that meant those who did not speak Greek, and then twice says they showed 'extraordinary kindness,' verse 2, and 'honored us in many ways,' verse 10. The chief official, Publius, held a title that is attested in inscriptions from the island. The offering of hospitality for three days to a whole company of shipwrecked travellers is a significant cost.

Puteoli, in the Bay of Naples, was Italy's main port for Egyptian grain and for travellers from the East. It had a Jewish community and, as verse 14 shows, Christians already. From there the Appian Way ran north to Rome. The BSB footnote gives the Forum of Appius as about 43 miles from Rome and the Three Taverns about 35. Believers had walked that distance to meet a man whom they knew only by his letter, and perhaps by Priscilla and Aquila, Acts 18:2 and Romans 16:3.

The Jewish community in Rome was large and had been shaken by Claudius's edict expelling Jews, Acts 18:2. The leaders in verse 21 say that no letters about Paul have come from Judea, which fits what we might expect: his accusers had to get a case to Caesar's court before Paul was heard. Paul's custody, verse 16, was the form of house arrest in which a soldier was chained to the prisoner, which is why he speaks of wearing a chain, verse 20.

The two years of verse 30 most likely run from about AD 60 to 62. Early Christian tradition holds that Paul was released, travelled again and was later executed under Nero, which would fit the shape of 2 Timothy 4:6 to 8, but Luke does not tell us. The letters traditionally dated to this imprisonment, Philippians, Ephesians, Colossians and Philemon, show what he did there, and Philippians 4:22 mentions believers in Caesar's household.
context.canonical:
Acts 28 is where several lines of the Old and New Testaments arrive together. The first is the line of the nations. God told Abraham that 'all the families of the earth will be blessed through you,' Genesis 12:3, and Isaiah's Servant is given as 'a light for the nations, to bring My salvation to the ends of the earth,' Isaiah 49:6. Paul applied that verse to his own mission in Acts 13:47, and now verse 28 uses the word 'salvation' in the sense Simeon gave it: 'a light for revelation to the Gentiles,' Luke 2:30 to 32. Luke 3:6 had said, quoting Isaiah, that 'all humanity will see God's salvation.' Acts 28:28 is the last stage of that sentence.

The second is the line of Israel's hardening. Isaiah 6:9 to 10 is quoted in all four Gospels and Acts in one form or another: Matthew 13:14 and 15 uses the same Septuagint wording Paul uses here, and John 12:37 to 41 pairs it with Isaiah 53:1 to explain why even signs did not persuade. Paul himself takes up the subject at length in Romans 9 to 11, where Israel's stumbling is real but not final, Romans 11:11 and 25 to 26.

The third is the line of the kingdom. Jesus had spoken of the kingdom of God for forty days after His resurrection, Acts 1:3, and Philip, Paul and others preached it in the book, Acts 8:12, 14:22, 19:8 and 20:25. The final verse makes the kingdom and the Lord Jesus Christ one message.

The fourth is the chain. Paul writes from imprisonment elsewhere that his chains advance the gospel, Philippians 1:12 to 14, that he is 'an ambassador in chains,' Ephesians 6:20, and that 'the word of God cannot be chained,' 2 Timothy 2:9. The last verse of Acts is the narrative form of that last claim.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Luke wrote Acts as the second part of an orderly account for Theophilus, Luke 1:1 to 4, so that he might know the certainty of what he had been taught. The ending serves that purpose. Luke wants his reader to be sure of three things. The gospel really is going out from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth, and has reached the centre of the empire. Paul's imprisonment is not the defeat of the mission but one of the ways it advances, which Luke shows by the freedom to preach that accompanies the chain. And the division among Israel, which the reader may find painful, is not a failure of God's word, since it was foreseen by Isaiah and the Spirit.

He also wants the reader to see a continuity between Jesus and the church. Acts 1:1 speaks of 'all that Jesus began to do and to teach,' and Acts 28 shows the same Jesus still teaching and healing through those He has sent. The closing picture is meant to leave Theophilus, and us, standing where the apostles stood: with an open door and a word that is not bound.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes events: a snakebite that did not harm Paul, healings on Malta, a meeting with Roman Jews and a division among them. It does not make a rule that believers will be immune to venom or that every sick person prayed for will recover. Paul himself left Trophimus ill at Miletus, 2 Timothy 4:20, and Luke's own account in Acts 12:2 is of a man killed. The signs of Acts 28 are works of the kingdom that authenticate the messenger and show mercy to strangers.

The Isaiah quotation is likewise a record of what Paul said on that day, not a permanent verdict. The last verses of Acts do not say that Jews are shut out, and Paul himself writes in Romans 11:1 that God has not rejected His people. What does carry forward is the pattern: the gospel is proclaimed to everyone who will hear, and it is both received and refused. Believers are meant to preach the kingdom 'from morning to evening' when needed, to persuade from the Scriptures, and to leave the outcome with God, who is still adding people to Himself. The picture of the open, unfinished ending is itself an instruction: the story goes on in the life of the church.

debates.question: Why does Acts end so abruptly, without telling us what happened to Paul?

views.label: The book's true subject is the gospel, not Paul
views.case: Luke set out to show the word of God advancing from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth, Acts 1:8; reaching Rome with the message preached boldly and unhindered completes that aim, so the story ends on the triumph of the word rather than the fate of one man, and the final word, unhindered, is the deliberate climax.

views.label: Luke wrote before the outcome was known
views.case: Others hold that Luke simply finished his account around AD 62, before Paul's trial was decided, so the ending reflects the state of things at the time of writing; on this view the abruptness is historical circumstance more than literary design, though it still leaves the gospel visibly advancing.

debates.bearing: Both readings agree the focus falls on the unstoppable progress of the word, not on closure for Paul. The open ending invites every later reader to see the mission as unfinished and to take up the same task; whether by design or circumstance, Acts leaves the gospel running free and hands the story on to the church.

debates.question: Does Paul's declaration in verse 28 mean God has finished with Israel?

views.label: A final judicial turn from Israel to the Gentiles
views.case: Some read Acts 28:25 to 28 as the closing verdict on the Jewish people: the Isaiah text of hardening is the last word and the Gentiles take the place that Israel refused. On this view the book ends with the church as the community of salvation and the nation as such set aside.

views.label: One more local turn in a continuing pattern
views.case: Others note that Paul has said the same thing at Antioch and Corinth, Acts 13:46 and 18:6, and then gone straight into the next synagogue. Luke says some in Rome were persuaded, verse 24, and that Paul welcomed 'all who came,' verse 30. In Romans 11:1 and 25 to 26 Paul denies that God has rejected Israel and speaks of a hardening in part until the full number of the Gentiles has come in.

debates.bearing: The second reading fits Paul's own letters better and Luke's pattern of turning, but the first sees something real: the movement of the gospel's centre of gravity toward the nations. A safe reading honours both. Salvation is now going out to everyone, and it remains true that the gospel is 'to the Jew first,' Romans 1:16, and that God has not abandoned His promises to His people.

study.originalLanguages:
Luke's choice of verbs in the Rome scene shows what Paul was doing and how the Jewish leaders responded. In verse 23 Paul 'expounded,' a word that means to set something out in order and lay it open, the same verb used of Peter explaining the whole sequence of events in Acts 11:4 and of Priscilla and Aquila explaining the way of God to Apollos in Acts 18:26. Alongside it Paul 'testified,' with the intensive verb diamartyromai that Paul uses of his entire ministry in Acts 20:24, 'testifying to the good news of God's grace.' Here at the end the testimony reaches the capital.

The verb for 'persuading,' peitho, is repeated in verse 24 in the passive: 'some were convinced.' The others 'refused to believe,' with apisteo, the verb for disbelief. Luke uses persuading for Paul's work elsewhere, as when he 'spoke boldly' and 'argued persuasively' about the kingdom in Ephesus, Acts 19:8. The language shows that Luke sees faith as a response to reasoned, scriptural teaching, not as an irrational leap and not as an automatic result.

The Isaiah quotation in verses 26 and 27 follows the Septuagint, the Greek version, rather than the Hebrew of Isaiah 6:9 and 10. In the Hebrew, the prophet is told, 'Make the hearts of this people calloused.' In the Greek, and in Acts, the people themselves have made their hearts callous and closed their eyes, and God says 'I would heal them.' The BSB footnote at verse 27 notes the dependence on the Septuagint. The difference is subtle but important: Luke emphasises responsibility on the hearers' side while retaining the sense that the word of the Lord has been spoken.

Verse 28 says salvation 'has been sent,' using apostello in the passive. The word of sending is the root of 'apostle.' Salvation itself is sent out as an apostle is sent out. The word translated 'salvation' here is soterion, the neuter form that Luke also uses at Luke 2:30 and 3:6, where God's salvation is something people see. And the final promise of the verse, 'they will listen,' is the verb akouo, to hear, the very word that fills Isaiah's complaint about people 'ever hearing.' The Gentiles do what Isaiah's generation would not.

Finally, verse 30 says Paul lived in his own 'hired dwelling,' which can mean either the rent he paid or the house itself, and welcomed 'all who came,' using an imperfect verb that pictures the welcome happening again and again. The last verse has two participles, 'proclaiming' and 'teaching,' both in the present tense, so that the book ends on continuing action, and the last Greek word is the adverb for 'without hindrance,' an adverb that simply says nothing stood in the way.

typology.type: The serpent that cannot kill, Acts 28:3 to 6
typology.fulfillment: The first promise in Scripture sets a seed of the woman against the serpent, who bruises his heel but is crushed, Genesis 3:15. Psalm 91:13 says of the one under God's protection, 'You will tread on the lion and cobra.' Jesus gives His disciples authority 'to tread on snakes and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy,' Luke 10:19, and the longer ending of Mark, which some early manuscripts omit, speaks of picking up snakes, Mark 16:18. Luke does not draw the connection, so this is an echo, not a declared type. Its escalation is that the victory over the serpent is won on the cross, and the church shares it. The type falls short because the viper on Malta is only a snake; the real enemy is judged by Christ, Colossians 2:15.

typology.type: The light for the Gentiles, Acts 28:28
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah's Servant is called a light for the nations to carry God's salvation to the ends of the earth, Isaiah 49:6, and to open blind eyes and free prisoners, Isaiah 42:6 to 7. Simeon identified the child Jesus with that light, Luke 2:30 to 32. Paul and Barnabas took the commission on themselves at Antioch, Acts 13:47. In Acts 28 the servant of the Servant is a prisoner who brings light to the capital. The fulfilment is in Christ alone, who is the light; Paul's role is a shared participation in it, Acts 26:18.

typology.type: The healer who lays on hands, Acts 28:8 to 9
typology.fulfillment: A man with fever is healed by prayer and the laying on of hands, and then the rest of the island's sick come. That is the shape of Jesus' day in Capernaum, when He rebuked a fever in Simon's house and at sunset laid hands on each of the sick, Luke 4:38 to 40. Acts begins by describing what Jesus 'began to do and to teach,' Acts 1:1, and the healing on Malta shows that He continues. The type falls short because Paul heals in the name of another, and because physical healing, however real, points to a deeper restoration. The final cure is the new creation, where the leaves of the tree are for the healing of the nations, Revelation 22:2.

typology.type: The prisoner who sets others free, Acts 28:16 to 20
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah 61:1, taken up by Jesus in Luke 4:18, announces freedom for prisoners. The apostle who preaches in chains shows that this freedom is not the same as the removal of bars. Paul calls himself the prisoner of Christ Jesus, Philemon 1:1 and Ephesians 3:1, and finds the gospel moving through his confinement, Philippians 1:12 to 14. The fulfilment is in Christ who was bound and raised, and the type falls short because Paul remains in a Roman cell until his work is done, while Christ breaks the chains of death.

study.christ:
The close of Acts brings Jesus into view through three phrases in its last scene. Paul 'persuaded them about Jesus from the Law of Moses and the Prophets,' verse 23. That is the way the risen Lord Himself taught the disciples on the Emmaus road and in the upper room: 'Everything must be fulfilled that is written about Me in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms,' Luke 24:44. The 'hope of Israel' for which Paul wears the chain, verse 20, is not a vague national expectation. In Acts 23:6 and 26:6 to 8 he explains it as the hope of resurrection and the promise made to the fathers, and in Acts 26:22 and 23 he says it is that 'the Christ would suffer, and as the first to rise from the dead, would proclaim light to our people and to the Gentiles.' The chain is on Paul's wrist because the Messiah has risen.

Second, the Isaiah passage is itself a Christ passage. John 12:41 says that Isaiah spoke of this hardening 'because he saw Jesus' glory and spoke about Him,' and Acts 28:25 says the Holy Spirit spoke it through Isaiah. The vision of Isaiah 6, in which the prophet sees the Lord on the throne, is therefore the vision of the Son, spoken by the Spirit, and applied by Paul in Rome. The refusal to hear is a refusal of Him.

Third, the closing words join the kingdom and the person: Paul proclaims the kingdom of God and teaches about 'the Lord Jesus Christ.' In Caesar's own city, where Caesar was Lord, the open proclamation that Jesus is Lord is the gospel's boldest claim. The charge Luke recorded in Thessalonica, 'there is another king, named Jesus,' Acts 17:7, is now preached in the capital without hindrance, and there are saints in Caesar's household, Philippians 4:22.

Fourth, the healings continue what Jesus began. Acts 1:1 introduces the book as the story of what Jesus 'began' to do and teach, and in Malta the Lord who healed a fever in Capernaum is healing a fever through His servant.

It is important not to over-read. The viper is not a code for Satan in Luke's text, and Publius's father is not a type of anyone. What the chapter gives is the risen Christ at work through His word and His servants, the same Lord who said, 'I am with you always,' Matthew 28:20, and who sends salvation to the nations.
study.god:
The God of Acts 28 is the God who keeps a promise made years earlier on a night in the barracks, Acts 23:11, and who is shown to have kept it with an almost understated precision. Paul, who has been shipwrecked, bitten and chained, arrives in Rome and Luke says only, 'And so we came to Rome,' verse 14. The words carry no triumph, because the triumph is God's.

He is the God who works through those who do not know Him. The people who feed and warm the survivors are the non-Greek speakers of an island, the benefactor is Publius, and their first judgment of Paul is mistaken in both directions. God's care is wider than the church, and His kindness comes to His people by Gentile hands, as it earlier did through the centurion Julius, Acts 27:3.

He is a God of both mercy and judgment, held together without contradiction. The healing of Publius's father and of the island's sick shows tender mercy toward those who are not His people. The Isaiah text shows judicial hardening on those who have heard and refused. Luke does not resolve how the two relate. He allows both to stand: the Gentiles 'will listen,' and some Jews are persuaded, while others turn away.

He is the God of the Spirit-inspired Scripture. Paul says, 'The Holy Spirit was right when He spoke to your fathers through Isaiah the prophet,' verse 25, as earlier believers said of David, Acts 1:16 and 4:25. The same prophecy is said in John 12:41 to be about Jesus, and in Isaiah 6 it is the voice of the Lord on the throne. The one text is spoken by the Spirit, seen by the prophet and applied to the Son, which is the Bible's way of showing a God who is one and yet speaks as Father, Son and Spirit.

He is the God whose word cannot be bound, Acts 6:7, 12:24 and 19:20. The last verse shows a chained man and a free message. That is the claim of 2 Timothy 2:9, and the book ends there on purpose.

For worship, the chapter calls us to do what Paul did when he met the believers from Rome: 'he was encouraged and gave thanks to God,' verse 15. Gratitude for the fellowship of other believers is gratitude to God, and a church is one of the ways God keeps His promises to His servants.

crossReferences.note: The Lord told Paul in the barracks that he would testify in Rome. Acts 28:14 to 16 is the arrival that fulfils this, and verses 23 to 31 show the testimony itself. The promise had survived a conspiracy, two governors and a storm.

Before He ascended, Jesus spoke to the apostles about the kingdom of God. The final verse of Acts has Paul proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ. The two phrases form an inclusio around the whole book, showing that the message at the end is the same as at the beginning.

At Pisidian Antioch Paul says the word had to be spoken to the Jews first and then turns to the Gentiles, citing Isaiah 49:6. Acts 28:28 is the third and final statement of the same turn, and the earlier one shows that the turn never meant that Jews would no longer be reached.

The text that Paul quotes in verses 26 and 27. Isaiah was sent to a people who would hear without understanding. The Greek form Paul uses has the people closing their own eyes, which stresses their responsibility, and it ends with God's offer to heal those who turn.

John uses the same Isaiah passage to explain why many did not believe in Jesus even after signs, and adds that Isaiah saw Jesus' glory and spoke of Him. This makes Paul's Isaiah quotation a statement about the Messiah, not just about an ancient generation.

Simeon holds the infant Jesus and calls Him God's salvation, a light for revelation to the Gentiles and glory for Israel. The salvation sent to the Gentiles in Acts 28:28 is that same salvation, and the book closes the loop the Gospel opened.

Jesus rebukes a fever in Simon's house and then lays hands on each of the sick at sunset. The healing of Publius's father and the arrival of the island's sick in Acts 28:8 and 9 follow the same order, which fits Luke's description of Acts as what Jesus continues to do.

Paul explains that Israel's stumbling is not a fall beyond recovery, and that salvation coming to the Gentiles is meant to provoke Israel to jealousy. This is a theological commentary on the turn of Acts 28:28.

Writing from imprisonment, Paul says his circumstances have advanced the gospel, that his chains are known throughout the palace guard and that other believers speak more boldly because of them. It shows what the two years of Acts 28:30 produced.

'The word of God cannot be chained.' Paul says this while suffering as a criminal. The last verse of Acts shows it in narrative form: a man in custody welcomes all, and the last word is that the proclamation goes on without hindrance.

Paul had hoped for years to see Rome on his way to Spain. He arrives in a way he did not plan, as a prisoner, but he arrives, and the church comes out to meet him. The letter and the narrative together show how God fulfilled a desire by an unexpected road.

study.oneStory:
Genesis 12 gave the Bible its plot: God would bless all the families of the earth through Abraham's seed, Genesis 12:3. The rest of the Old Testament follows a people who are meant to carry that blessing and repeatedly fail, until Isaiah hears the Servant be told that restoring Israel is too small a task: 'I will also make You a light for the nations,' Isaiah 49:6. Luke's two volumes are the story of that Servant and His witnesses. The Gospel ends in Jerusalem with the command that repentance and forgiveness be proclaimed 'to all nations, beginning in Jerusalem,' Luke 24:47, and Acts 1:8 maps the road: Jerusalem, Judea and Samaria, and the ends of the earth.

Acts 28 is where the map reaches the heart of the Gentile world. It is not the end of the mission. Paul speaks of Spain, Romans 15:24, and the book simply stops while the gospel runs on. In that sense the whole history of the church since is a continuation of the last verse of Acts.

The chapter also holds the tension that the rest of the Bible keeps open: Israel's unbelief in part and the Gentiles' welcome. Paul will say in Romans 11 that this is a mystery with a conclusion, 'a hardening in part has come to Israel, until the full number of the Gentiles has come in,' Romans 11:25, and that God has not rejected His people. The Spirit's use of Isaiah's hard words is not the last word of the story, but one scene in a plot God is still writing.

It anticipates the end as well. Revelation 7:9 pictures 'a multitude too large to count, from every nation and tribe and people and tongue, standing before the throne and before the Lamb.' Every Gentile who 'will listen' in Acts 28:28 is a first fruit of that crowd. And the healed of Malta and the preached-to of Rome point to the day when the tree of life has leaves 'for the healing of the nations,' Revelation 22:2. Until then, the story is in the hands of the church, with a message that no chain can bind.

quiz.q: What is the significance of the open, unfinished ending of Acts?

options.text: The focus is the unstoppable advance of the gospel, left running so the church continues the mission.
options.note: Luke ends on the word preached boldly and unhindered, the true subject of the book, not Paul's fate.

options.text: Luke may have written before the outcome of Paul's trial was known.
options.note: A reasonable historical explanation, but it still leaves the emphasis on the gospel's ongoing progress rather than closure for Paul.

options.text: Luke ran out of information about Paul's later life.
options.note: This underestimates the deliberate design; the ending fits Luke's stated aim of the word reaching the ends of the earth.

options.text: The ending shows the mission had failed in Rome.
options.note: The opposite; the gospel is preached freely and openly, a note of triumph, not failure.

quiz.q: How did the islanders of Malta interpret the viper on Paul's hand?

options.text: First that he was a murderer being punished, then that he was a god when he was unharmed.
options.note: They swung from one superstition to the other, verses 4 and 6, while God simply preserved His servant.

options.text: That he was a murderer whom Justice would not let live.
options.note: True of their first reaction, but they later reversed and called him a god.

options.text: That the bite was an accident of no meaning.
options.note: They read deep meaning into it, first condemnation, then divinity; they did not treat it as meaningless.

options.text: That Paul had tamed the snake by magic.
options.note: They said nothing about magic; they concluded he must be a god.

quiz.q: How did the Jewish leaders in Rome respond to Paul's teaching about Jesus?

options.text: Some were convinced, but others refused to believe, and they left divided.
options.note: Luke records a split response, verses 24 to 25, the mixed reception that runs through Acts.

options.text: They all rejected his message and drove him away.
options.note: Not all rejected it; some were convinced, though the group left in disagreement.

options.text: They all believed and were baptized.
options.note: The response was divided, not a wholesale conversion.

options.text: They reported him to Caesar as a troublemaker.
options.note: Nothing of the kind; they had received no charges against him and came to hear his views.

quiz.q: What does Paul announce after quoting Isaiah's warning?

options.text: That God's salvation has been sent to the Gentiles, and they will listen.
options.note: Paul declares the turn to the Gentiles, verse 28, a key theme of the whole book.

options.text: That the hearts of the people have grown callous.
options.note: That is Isaiah's warning he quotes, verse 27, but his announcement that follows is the sending of salvation to the Gentiles.

options.text: That Israel has been permanently cast off by God.
options.note: Paul does not say Israel is cast off; some believed, and elsewhere he holds out hope for his people.

options.text: That he will stop preaching to everyone.
options.note: The opposite; he keeps preaching boldly for two more years to all who come.

quiz.q: How does the book of Acts describe Paul's preaching at its very end?

options.text: He proclaimed the kingdom of God and taught about the Lord Jesus Christ boldly and without hindrance.
options.note: The final verse ends on the word unhindered, the triumphant close of the book, verse 31.

options.text: He welcomed all who came to visit him in his rented house.
options.note: True, verse 30, but the climactic note is the bold, unhindered preaching of Christ.

options.text: He preached quietly and in secret to avoid trouble.
options.note: The opposite; he spoke openly and boldly, without hindrance.

options.text: He gave up preaching while awaiting his trial.
options.note: He did not give up; he proclaimed Christ freely throughout the two years.

questions: Acts ends with the gospel still on the move and the story left open. How does it change your sense of purpose to know you are part of a mission that is not yet finished?
Paul was chained, yet the word of God was not hindered. Where do your own limits or circumstances tempt you to think the gospel is stuck, when God can still work freely?
The seaside islanders showed extraordinary kindness, and Paul repaid it with healing and witness. How might ordinary hospitality, given or received, open a door for the gospel?
When Paul saw the Roman brothers on the road, he was encouraged and gave thanks to God. Who has God placed in your life to strengthen you, and have you thanked Him for them?
Paul kept preaching Christ boldly through two uncertain years. Where is God calling you to steady, faithful witness even when the outcome is unclear?

translationNotes.note: The BSB omits verse 29, following the earliest and best Greek manuscripts, which move from verse 28 to verse 30. A footnote records that the later Byzantine text and Received Text add: When he had said this, the Jews went away, disputing sharply among themselves. Because the sentence is absent from the oldest manuscripts, the verse number is left unused. We carry the omission faithfully.

Paul quotes Isaiah 6:9 to 10, the same prophecy Jesus applied to hardened hearers. It explains Israel's divided response without denying God's continuing purpose, and it frames the sending of salvation to the Gentiles.

The final phrase renders two Greek terms: with parrhesia, boldness or openness, and akolytos, without hindrance, which is the very last word of the book. Luke ends deliberately on the unstoppable freedom of the gospel, even while Paul remains a prisoner.
